name: Bone marrow / bone broth

lead: Bone broth is stock made by simmering bones and connective tissue for a long time; bone marrow is the fatty tissue inside long bones, eaten roasted or in soups. Both are used in wellness and looksmaxxing circles for collagen, with users hoping for firmer skin and healthier joints.

The chain is that simmering releases collagen, which turns into gelatin, supplying collagen building blocks for skin and joints. Bone broth became a wellness trend in the early 2010s; Wikipedia reports there is no scientific evidence to support many of the claims made for it, and no published trial was found testing it for skin or appearance.

paras: Broth is simmered for hours with bones, vegetables and herbs and drunk as a warm drink or used as a soup base; marrow is roasted and eaten on bread or stirred into dishes. Users often make it a regular daily or weekly habit.

Broth and marrow are ordinary foods generally not regarded as risky for most people. Marrow is high in fat, and bones can concentrate contaminants in some preparations. Vertebral spinal marrow is banned for sale in some countries, including the UK, because of mad cow disease concerns.

web.title: Is the collagen in bone broth good for your skin and joints? - Which?

angle.text: Bone broth and marrow are consumed for their collagen, with users hoping for firmer skin and healthier joints. Both are long-standing foods, and no published trials examine appearance.

lead: Bone broth is a cooking liquid made by simmering bones, often with meat scraps, vegetables and herbs, for an extended period. During simmering, collagen in bones and connective tissue turns into gelatin, which thickens the liquid [1]. Bone marrow is the edible tissue inside long bones, found in yellow and red forms, and has been eaten for a very long time [2]. People in wellness and looksmaxxing circles take them as a skin-and-joint food: the idea is that the collagen, gelatin and amino acids in broth feed firmer, plumper-looking skin and comfortable joints that support training [1][3].

Health claims about bone broth became popular in the early 2010s, helped by books such as Nourishing Broth (2014), and bone broth bars and delivery services grew in the United States [1]. Within appearance communities, broth is promoted alongside collagen powders for skin, hair and nails, and marrow is eaten for fat and nutrients [2].

A 2025 review in Digestive Diseases and Sciences examined the amino acids (glutamine, glycine, proline, histidine, arginine) and minerals in bone broth and reported that animal and human studies on these components support gut-barrier function and reduced intestinal inflammation [3]. Reference sources state that digested collagen is broken into peptides and amino acids rather than incorporated intact into skin, and a 2025 summary in Wikipedia's collagen article reports no clinical evidence that oral collagen supplements improve wrinkles or skin ageing [4]. Wikipedia's bone broth article says there is no scientific evidence supporting many of the claims made for it [1]. No published trial has tested bone broth or marrow for skin appearance.

paras: Stock is a savoury cooking liquid made by simmering bones, meat, seafood or vegetables, and bone broth is another name for bone-based stock. Bones and connective tissue release collagen that becomes gelatin, so bone-based stocks are usually thicker than meat-based broths [1].

Bone marrow is sold in bone-in cuts and is eaten in many cuisines, such as phở in Vietnam, bulalo in the Philippines, nalli nihari in India and Pakistan, and ossobuco in Italy. Red marrow is reported to contain more nutrients than yellow marrow [2].

Some anthropologists think early humans cracked bones to reach marrow, with stone tools used for this going back almost 2 million years, and Neanderthals rendering marrow fat about 125,000 years ago [2]. In 18th century Europe diners used special marrow scoops, and marrow now appears in some restaurant dishes [2].
The modern wellness trend dates from the early 2010s, and a 2019 scene from The Mandalorian in which a character sips broth became an internet meme [1].

sections.h: Nutrients and what is known about them
paras: A 2025 review describes bone broth as a source of glutamine, glycine, proline, histidine and arginine plus calcium, phosphorus, potassium, magnesium and zinc, and concludes from animal and human studies of these components that they support intestinal barrier integrity and may help in inflammatory bowel disease [3]. The review concerns gut health, not skin.

Collagen is the structural protein of skin, and when ingested it is digested into hydrolysed peptides and amino acids, so the intact protein is not incorporated into skin directly, though its constituents might be [4]. Wikipedia reports there is no good evidence that eating collagen affects collagen production or skin health and that, as of 2025, no clinical evidence shows oral collagen supplements improving wrinkles [4]. Consumer-health coverage adds that the collagen content of homemade and commercial broths varies from batch to batch and is not usually listed on labels [5].

Proponents in wellness and ancestral-diet communities say broth supplies collagen, gelatin and minerals that support skin, joints and gut lining; these are the claims behind its use as a skin food [1]. On T Nation, members discuss making broth from bones, aiming for a gelatinous set, and one describes cracking chicken bones to eat the marrow [6][7].

No studies found testing bone broth or bone marrow consumption for skin, hair or appearance outcomes. Related research exists on broth's amino acids and gut barrier function [3], and on collagen supplements as a separate category, where Wikipedia's collagen article reports no clinical evidence of skin benefit as of 2025 [4].

lore.intro: Bone broth and marrow come up in strength and ancestral-diet forums mainly as foods for joints, gut and general nutrition, with skin mentioned as a hoped-for benefit.

claims.claim: Eating collagen-rich broth makes skin firmer and younger-looking.
Bone broth supports gut lining and reduces inflammation.
Marrow is a nutrient-dense food worth eating.
